When and How quickly will self driving cars replace regular cars?

Quite rapidly. The costs will not be substantially greater than conventional vehicles. The biggest expense is software but the nice thing about software is that once it's designed, it's effectively free to reproduce. The detection systems and mechanical implementations are not exactly future era tech. It's just a matter of giving them 'brains.' Governments will likely also subsidize the costs for the vehicles. Once widely implemented self driving vehicles will dramatically reduce traffic, traffic related deaths and injuries, and much more.

These are macro level appeals. Everybody thinks they're a good driver so they'll assume stuff like reducing traffic related injuries and so on won't apply to them but there will also be plenty of micro level stuff as well. Instead of spending your morning road raging rush hour you can kick back and watch a movie or just take a nap. Or when you feel like going out and having some drinks you can bring your car, have it come pick you up when you're ready to go home using a tablet app, and then safely get home without a problem or posing a danger to yourself or anybody else. Road trip? Plug in the destination, and make sure you brought a couple of books.

We'll also likely see governments begin to ban manually controlled vehicles in city areas. This won't actually be as disruptive as you might think. A self driving solar/electric vehicle will be able to operate for next to nothing. You're going to to see this translate into dirt cheap taxis you can pick up from and to anywhere. The current CEO of uber has already publicly stated he'd like to buy the entirety of Tesla's first line of self driving vehicles, estimated at 500,000 in 2020. That's one man with a fleet of 500,000 taxis. Bad news for the mass unemployment it'll entail, but the possibilities this all opens up are amazing. We just need to prep our economic system for an increasingly irrelevant labor force.

People keep saying that they're spooked by the concept of a self-driving car, that they would have little to no control over it and that scares people. A few points I think will help settle the debate:

  • People were just as scared when the first automobiles came around. They were scared of speed. They had very heavy regulations. They were expensive. Nobody could see themselves owning one, or the fad catching on. Sounds familiar? That's because it's what people are saying about it now.

  • The technology is only getting better and safer. Think about digital music in the 90's. The technology was there, but the public mindset and the legislation were not, so it didn't catch on. That is, until, some guys named Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak came along and invented iTunes. Developed the DRM to make record labels happy, while keeping the price point low enough for consumers to pay and not pirate. I propose that the technology for self-driving cars already exists, is getting better, and all we need is one company to come along (Tesla Motors?) and do it right, because that's all it would take. Put in the right amount of technology, safety, and legislation, and suddenly you reach critical mass.

  • There are multiple possible levels of ownership. You could try and purchase or lease a self-driving car, but what if you used it like public transit? A company like Uber could easily integrate self-driving cars into their network. You pay different rates based on distance, car size, and whether or not you carpool. You subscribe to Uber for your morning commute, and suddenly you're commuting in an SUV every morning with 5 of your coworkers, none of you are driving, all of you are already working. It doesn't have to be Uber either, it could be full-on tax-funded public transit.

  • Think efficiency. We have this fleet of self driving cars. Suddenly they can take themselves in for an oil change, get gas, recharge, whatever. You have to stay late at work? Your car picks up the kids from school, then comes back to you when you're ready to leave. A family of four could possibly only need to own one family car, since the car could be doing other things while you're working. Rush hour suddenly doesn't exist, as most cars on the road are self-driving: they route more efficiently to their destinations, they're more predictable of each other than a human driver, they regulate speed and follow distance better than humans, and people would be carpooling more so there would be less cars on the road in the first place. You personally could gain a full hour of your day back, instead of being focused on the road while in-transit.

These are the reasons why everyone is talking about self-driving cars. Why everyone from Google to Tesla to your mother is working on self-driving cars. The implications are enormous. This isn't like the 3DTV fad. This isn't like the motion controls in video games fad. This is a legitimate groundbreaking technology which has huge implications for increasing societal productivity and reducing environmental impact.

I see this going full-scale by about 2030. (Which coincidentally is roughly when the movie "I Robot" takes place, and that movie has a very realistic depiction of how self-driving cars could function.)

I'll never own a self-driving car, for the following reasons

  • The lack of privacy is overwhelming. These cars, especially Google autonomous cars, like to be connected to some form of network at all times. This is not bueno, and I will never consent to such an infringement. We live in an age where you would be completely retarded NOT to assume that everything about your Googlecar is collecting metrics on you, and delivering it all straight to the powers that be. I mean shit, this is a stretch, but what's to stop the government from using these as a tool for their assassination programs? All they would need is access to the car's network, and if you're someone they don't like, they could send you off a cliff at a whim. That sounds like a Doctor Who episode, but it's certainly not outside the realm of probability.

  • They're not fun. Nothing about autopilot is fun. I'm one of those rare breeds who actually enjoys driving and working on mechanical vehicles. I work in a car dealership, I daily drive a mail truck, and I'm restoring my first car (a Volkswagen Superbeetle). Autonomy is not welcome anywhere near myself, or my group of friends.

  • Modification will not be an option. The big three, and nearly all Japanese and German marques have banded together to pitch legislation that would make it a felony to modify the software, hardware, or most anything about new cars themselves, autonomous or not. I don't like samey. I don't like cookie-cutter. All new cars are the same fucking thing anyway. Most importantly, it's my fucking property and you're telling me I can't do what I want with it.

  • Autonomous Vehicles are not here for your benefit. Think about it. Think about every other ground transportation method that sprouted up in the past, and played with the dominance of the automobile. The GM EV-1, the early 20th century Detroit Electric Streetcar system, the original autonomous cars made by DARPA. All have been met with HUGE opposition from Big Auto. The two first examples were destroyed single handedly by General Motors, so why aren't they putting up a fight about autonomous vehicles of the nowtimes, if they don't have a stake in it? These cars are not made for you. They're meant to take advantage of you.
